items.readable_text:
Content:
In this lesson, we'll learn how to determine trigonometric ratios of large angles in radians.

Content:
For example, suppose we wish to find the value of

Content:
[MATH: \sin\left(\dfrac{203\pi}{4}\right).]

Content:
Trigonometric ratios like sine and cosine repeat every [MATH: 2\pi] radians (full turns). So, instead of evaluating a large angle directly, we reduce it to a smaller, coterminal angle between [MATH: 0] and
[MATH: 2\pi.] To do this, we write the angle as a sum of multiples of [MATH: 2\pi] plus a remainder.

Content:
We first find an angle that's coterminal with [MATH: \dfrac{203\pi}{4}] and lies in the range [MATH: [0,2\pi).]

Content:
Recall that coterminal angles differ by a multiple of [MATH: 2\pi] radians.
So, we divide [MATH: 203] by [MATH: 2 \cdot 4 = 8] with remainder:

Content:
[MATH: 203 \div 8 = 25 \ \text{R} \ 3]

Content:
Therefore,
[MATH: 203 = 25 \cdot 8 + 3.]

Content:
As a result, we have

Content:
[MATH: (203π)/(4)|= ((25 ⋅ 8 + 3)π)/(4); = 25 ⋅ (8π)/(4) + (3π)/(4); = 25 ⋅ 2π + (3π)/(4).]

Content:
So, we can reduce our large angle of [MATH: \dfrac{203\pi}{4}] by [MATH: 25] full turns of [MATH: 2\pi,] as adding or subtracting a full turn doesn't change the sine:

Content:
[MATH: \sin \left(\dfrac{203\pi}{4}\right) = \sin \left({\color{blue}25 \cdot 2\pi} + \dfrac{3\pi}{4}\right) = \sin \left(\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\right)]

Content:
Let's remind ourselves of the special trigonometric ratios, as given by the unit circle.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/fe5847cb99ec31312e22032a3860e6bc]

Content:
From the unit circle, we see that the angle [MATH: \dfrac{3\pi}{4}] corresponds to the point [MATH: \left(-\dfrac{\sqrt 2}{2},\dfrac{\sqrt 2}{2}\right).]

Content:
Since the sine of the angle corresponds to the [MATH: y]-coordinate, we have [MATH: \sin\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\right) = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.]

Content:
Therefore,

Content:
[MATH: \sin\left(\dfrac{203\pi}{4}\right) = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}2.]

sections.normalized_html:
First, we find an angle that's coterminal with [MATH: \dfrac{127\pi}{6}] and lies in the range [MATH: [0,2\pi).]

Recall that coterminal angles differ by a multiple of [MATH: 2\pi] radians.

So, we divide [MATH: 127] by [MATH: 2 \cdot 6 = 12] with remainder:

[MATH: 127 \div 12 = 10 \ \text{R} \ 7]

Therefore, [MATH: 127 = 10 \cdot 12 + 7.]

As a result, we have

[MATH: (127π)/(6)|= ((10 ⋅ 12 + 7)π)/(6); = 10 ⋅ (12π)/(6) + (7π)/(6); = 10 ⋅ 2π + (7π)/(6).]

Therefore, [MATH: \sin \left(\dfrac{127\pi}{6}\right) = \sin \left(\dfrac{7\pi}{6}\right).]

Let's remind ourselves of the special trigonometric ratios, as given by the unit circle.

From the unit circle, we see that the angle [MATH: \dfrac{7\pi}{6}] corresponds to the point [MATH: \left(-\dfrac{\sqrt 3}{2},-\dfrac{1}{2}\right).]

Since the sine of the angle corresponds to the [MATH: y]-coordinate, we have [MATH: \sin\left(\dfrac{7\pi}{6}\right) = -\dfrac{1}{2}.]

Therefore, [MATH: \sin\left(\dfrac{127\pi}{6}\right) = -\dfrac{1}{2}.]

sections.normalized_html:
First, we find an angle that's coterminal with [MATH: \dfrac{159\pi}{4}] and lies in the range [MATH: [0,2\pi).]

Recall that coterminal angles differ by a multiple of [MATH: 2\pi] radians.

So, we divide [MATH: 159] by [MATH: 2 \cdot 4 = 8] with remainder:

[MATH: 159 \div 8 = 19 \ \text{R} \ 7]

Therefore, [MATH: 159 = 19 \cdot 8 + 7.]

As a result, we have

[MATH: (159π)/(4)|= ((19 ⋅ 8 + 7)π)/(4); = 19 ⋅ (8π)/(4) + (7π)/(4); = 19 ⋅ 2π + (7π)/(4).]

Therefore, [MATH: \cos \left(\dfrac{159\pi}{4}\right) = \cos \left(\dfrac{7\pi}{4}\right).]

Let's remind ourselves of the special trigonometric ratios, as given by the unit circle.

From the unit circle, we see that the angle [MATH: \dfrac{7\pi}{4}] corresponds to the point [MATH: \left(\dfrac{\sqrt 2}{2},-\dfrac{\sqrt 2}{2}\right).]

Since the cosine of the angle corresponds to the [MATH: x]-coordinate, we have [MATH: \cos \left(\dfrac{7\pi}{4}\right) = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.]

Therefore, [MATH: \cos\left(\dfrac{159\pi}{4}\right) = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.]

items.title: Finding the Tangent of a Large Angle

sections.normalized_html:
First, we find an angle that's coterminal with [MATH: \dfrac{215\pi}{4}] and lies in the range [MATH: [0,2\pi).]

Recall that coterminal angles differ by a multiple of [MATH: 2\pi] radians.

So, we divide [MATH: 215] by [MATH: 2 \cdot 4 = 8] with remainder:

[MATH: 215 \div 8 = 26 \ \text{R} \ 7]

Therefore, [MATH: 215 = 26 \cdot 8 + 7]

As a result, we have

[MATH: (215π)/(4)|= ((26 ⋅ 8 + 7)π)/(4); = 26 ⋅ (8π)/(4) + (7π)/(4); = 26 ⋅ 2π + (7π)/(4).]

Therefore, [MATH: \tan \left(\dfrac{215\pi}{4}\right) = \tan \left(\dfrac{7\pi}{4}\right).]

Let's remind ourselves of the special trigonometric ratios, as given by the unit circle.

From the unit circle, we see that the angle [MATH: \dfrac{7\pi}{4}] corresponds to the point [MATH: \left(\dfrac{\sqrt 2}{2}, -\dfrac{\sqrt 2}{2}\right).]

  • Since the cosine of the angle corresponds to the [MATH: x]-coordinate, we have [MATH: \cos \left( \dfrac{7\pi}{4}\right) = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.]

  • Since the sine of the angle corresponds to the [MATH: y]-coordinate, we have [MATH: \sin \left( \dfrac{7\pi}{4}\right) = -\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.]

Therefore, using the fact that [MATH: \tan\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta},] we have [MATH: \tan \left( \dfrac{7\pi}{4}\right) = \dfrac{\sin \left( \dfrac{7\pi}{4}\right)}{\cos\left( \dfrac{7\pi}{4}\right)} = \dfrac{-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}}{\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}} = -1.]
